_comment: One line about a day's destination, to give the email something to open with.
Written by hand rather than generated at send time: an unreviewed sentence
about a town nobody has checked is exactly the sort of thing that ends up
wrong in front of forty people who know John.
Coverage is deliberately partial. Where there is no entry the email simply
omits the line — a missing fact costs nothing, a wrong one costs trust.
Keyed by the destination name as it appears in itinerary.json.

facts.Nazaré: The waves off Praia do Norte are among the biggest ever surfed — an undersea canyon funnels Atlantic swell straight at the headland, and the record rides here have topped 80 feet.
facts.Porto: The port wine isn't aged in Porto. It crosses the river to the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia, where the cooler north-facing bank suits the barrels better.
facts.Pontevedra: Pontevedra threw cars out of its historic centre in 1999. Traffic deaths in the city fell to almost nothing, and it has been collecting urban planning awards ever since.
facts.A Coruña: The Tower of Hercules has been guiding ships since the Romans built it, making it the oldest lighthouse still working anywhere in the world.
facts.Burela: Burela's fleet lands more bonito tuna than almost anywhere in Spain, hauled in by hand-line one fish at a time.
facts.Puerto de Vega: A fishing village of a few hundred people, and the place where Jovellanos — the great Spanish Enlightenment reformer — died in 1811 while fleeing Napoleon's army.
facts.Oviedo: There is a life-size bronze statue of Woody Allen on a street corner here, put up after he called Oviedo one of the most beautiful cities in the world.
facts.Riaño: The village John rides into is not the old one. The original Riaño lies under the reservoir beside it, flooded in 1987 — in dry years the outline of the old town reappears.
facts.Burgos: El Cid is buried in the cathedral, which is the only one in Spain to be a UNESCO site in its own right rather than as part of a wider old town.
facts.Soria: Antonio Machado taught French here and wrote Campos de Castilla, the book that turned this stretch of high plain into some of the best-known landscape in Spanish poetry.
facts.Trasmoz: Trasmoz is the only village in Spain to have been formally excommunicated — and it is still cursed. Both were issued in the 13th century and neither has ever been lifted.
facts.Canfranc: Canfranc's railway station is a 200-metre Art Deco palace in the middle of the Pyrenees, built for traffic that never came and used during the war to move tungsten and refugees.
facts.Pau: Henry IV was born in the castle here. The town also runs a Grand Prix through its streets, one of the oldest street circuits still racing.
facts.Mende: Mende is the capital of Lozère, the least populated department in France — more cattle than people, and the emptiest sky in the country for stargazing.
facts.Chambéry: Once the capital of the Dukes of Savoy, before they moved to Turin. Its best-known landmark is a fountain of four elephants, paid for by a local who made a fortune in India.
facts.Aosta: The Romans built Augusta Praetoria here in 25 BC and the street grid has barely moved since. The valley still speaks French as well as Italian.
facts.Zermatt: No petrol cars are allowed in Zermatt. Everything runs on small electric vehicles, under the Matterhorn.
facts.Lauterbrunnen: Seventy-two waterfalls drop into this one valley. Tolkien walked here in 1911 and the landscape is widely reckoned to be the model for Rivendell.
facts.Andermatt: Andermatt sits at the crossroads of the great alpine passes — Furka, Oberalp, Gotthard — which is why armies, traders and one Bond car chase have all come through it.
facts.Davos: At 1,560 metres this is the highest town in Europe. Thomas Mann set The Magic Mountain in one of its sanatoriums, back when people came here to breathe rather than to talk economics.
facts.Innsbruck: Innsbruck has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1964 and 1976 — the second time at short notice, after Denver voted to hand the games back.
facts.Merano: A spa town where the Austro-Hungarian aristocracy came to take the air, Empress Sisi among them. Palm trees grow here despite the Alps on every side.
facts.Venice: Venice is built across 118 small islands, joined by around 400 bridges, on millions of wooden piles driven into the mud — which have held for a thousand years because they never see air.
facts.Duino: Rilke was staying at Duino Castle in 1912 when, walking the cliffs in a storm, he heard the first line of what became the Duino Elegies.
facts.Split: Split's old town is a Roman palace. Diocletian retired here in 305 AD, and when the empire collapsed people simply moved into it — the streets still follow his floor plan.
facts.Dubrovnik: The city walls run two kilometres around the old town and have never been breached. Dubrovnik was an independent republic for 450 years, playing off larger powers.
facts.Elbasan: Elbasan sits on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road that ran from the Adriatic to Byzantium — the route by which Rome reached the east, and roughly the one John is riding.
facts.Florina: Florina's red peppers are a protected designation in Greece, roasted and jarred across the country. The town also sits close to two national parks and Greece's brown bears.
facts.Thessaloniki: Greece's second city, and for centuries one of the great Jewish cities of Europe — Ladino was widely spoken in its streets into the 20th century.
facts.Kavala: A Roman aqueduct still runs across the middle of the town. Kavala was also the birthplace of Muhammad Ali, the Albanian-born soldier who founded modern Egypt's ruling dynasty.
facts.Istanbul: The only city in the world standing on two continents. John crosses from Europe into Asia here — the first of the seven, done.
